title: Recognise and manage stable and un-mounted vices in Equines

lessons.title: What vices are and why they develop
lessons.html:
Defining vices

A vice (also called a stereotypy or stable vice when it is repetitive) is an abnormal behaviour that a horse performs again and again, with no obvious purpose. Un-mounted vices are problem behaviours seen when the horse is being handled from the ground. Vices reduce a horse's value, can damage its health and equipment, and can injure people.

Common stable vices

ViceDescriptionPossible effects
Crib-bitingGrips a fixed object with the front teeth, arches the neck and gulps airAbnormal tooth wear, damage to stables; linked in studies to some forms of colic and gastric problems
Wind-suckingGulps air without gripping an objectSimilar to crib-biting
WeavingSwings the head and neck from side to side, shifting weight between forelegsUneven wear on legs and feet, weight loss, stress
Box-walkingWalks round and round the stableWeight loss, fatigue, churned bedding
Wood-chewingChews stable woodwork and fencesDamage, splinters; may indicate lack of fibre
Door-kicking and pawingKicks the door or paws the floor, often at feed timeInjury to legs and hooves, damage to doors
Rug-tearingTears off or chews rugsCost, risk of eating fabric

Common un-mounted vices

  • Biting and nipping
  • Kicking at people or other horses
  • Barging and pushing through people
  • Refusing to be caught, or pulling back when tied
  • Refusing to pick up feet, or to load
  • Rearing when led

Why vices develop

Horses evolved to live in herds, move constantly and graze for most of the day. Many vices develop when management prevents these needs:

  • Long hours in a stable with little turnout
  • Isolation from other horses
  • Low-forage, high-concentrate diets and long gaps between meals
  • Boredom, stress and frustration, for example at feed time
  • Early or abrupt weaning
  • Pain, for example gastric ulcers or dental problems
  • For handling vices: rough or inconsistent handling, fear, or pain from tack

A vice is a sign that the horse is struggling to cope. It is not "bad character".

lessons.title: Identifying and managing existing vices
lessons.html:
Identifying a vice

Watch the horse quietly without disturbing it, at different times of day. Look for signs:

  • Crib-biting: worn front teeth, bite marks on doors and mangers, a grunting sound
  • Weaving: a worn path at the door, sweating at the door
  • Box-walking: a circular track in the bedding
  • Wood-chewing: chewed edges on doors and rails

Record what, when and how often, and what seems to trigger it, such as feed time, other horses leaving, or being stabled alone. Report it to the yard manager. A vet check can rule out pain such as ulcers or teeth problems.

Managing established stable vices

Once a stereotypy is established it is often impossible to stop completely. The aim is to reduce it and its harmful effects, not to punish.

  • More turnout with companions where safe.
  • More forage: ad lib or more frequent hay, slow-feeder hay nets to extend eating time.
  • Lower concentrate and smaller, more frequent meals.
  • Company: a stable with a view of other horses; a grille between stables.
  • Enrichment: feed balls, licks, hanging vegetables as allowed.
  • Physical measures as the manager decides: anti-weave grilles, covering wood with metal strips, cribbing collars. These stop the behaviour but not the cause, and may increase stress; use only on advice.

Never punish a horse for a stereotypy. It increases stress and usually makes the behaviour worse.

Managing un-mounted vices

  1. Check for a cause: pain from tack, teeth, back or feet; fear from past handling.
  2. Handle consistently: all staff use the same commands and routines.
  3. Stay calm and assertive. Reward wanted behaviour immediately with release of pressure, a rub or a word.
  4. Correct dangerous behaviour such as biting firmly and immediately, but without anger or beating.
  5. Use safe equipment: a well-fitted headcollar or a bridle for leading difficult horses, gloves, a hard hat.
  6. Put warning notices on stables of horses that bite or kick.

Experienced staff should handle dangerous horses; less experienced staff should not be put at risk.

lessons.title: Preventing vices
lessons.html:
Prevention is better than cure

Because established vices are hard to remove, preventing them through good management is the most effective strategy. Prevention starts with the foal and continues throughout the horse's life.

Management practices that prevent vices

NeedPractice
MovementDaily turnout in a paddock or camp; regular exercise; avoid long periods of box rest unless the vet orders it
Social contactTurnout with compatible companions; stables where horses can see and smell each other
ForagingHigh-forage diet; hay available for most of the day; concentrates in small meals
RoutineRegular, predictable feeding and exercise times; reduce waiting and frustration at feed time
Low stressQuiet yard, gradual changes, calm handling
HealthRegular dental care, parasite control, prompt treatment of pain and ulcers

Youngstock

  • Wean gradually and in groups, for example by removing mares a few at a time from a group of mares and foals, rather than abruptly isolating a foal.
  • Keep weanlings in groups with plenty of forage and space.
  • Handle foals early, gently and consistently so they learn to lead, stand tied, and pick up feet without fear.

Preventing handling vices

  • Everyone in the yard uses the same, consistent methods.
  • Do not hand-feed treats in a way that teaches nipping.
  • Fit tack correctly so it does not cause pain.
  • Never hit a horse around the head; this creates head-shyness.
  • Reward calm, correct behaviour; keep sessions short and end on a good note.

Does copying happen?

Many people believe horses copy vices from their neighbours. Research has not clearly shown this. It is more likely that horses kept in the same poor conditions develop the same vices. Improving management for all horses is better than isolating a horse with a vice, which can make it worse.

Key points

  • Vices are repetitive abnormal behaviours that signal the horse is not coping.
  • Main causes are confinement, isolation, low forage, stress and pain.
  • Record and report vices and have the vet rule out pain.
  • Never punish stereotypies; increase turnout, forage and company.
  • Prevent vices with movement, companions, forage, routine and consistent, calm handling.
